mappings.note: Fourth angle from the 360 angle sum. Solving a numeric problem from a property of the figure -> C-4.1. C-7.3 rejected: nothing is proved, the angle sum is used as a given. This chapter's frame holds no learning outcomes, so competency level is the ceiling here.
Angles in the ratio 3:4:5:6 - computation from the angle sum. C-7.3 rejected, no deductive argument is asked for.
Acute angle between the diagonals of a rectangle from a 25 degree inclination. Uses equal diagonals and the isosceles triangle that follows, to compute a measure -> C-4.1 rather than C-7.3.
Rhombus, angle ACB = 40, find angle ADB: alternate angles plus perpendicular diagonals, used to compute. C-7.3 rejected - the properties are applied, not established.

Which condition on PQRS makes its mid-point quadrilateral a rectangle - exactly 'make and test conjectures'. C-7.3 rejected: the item selects the condition, it does not demand the proof (even though the stored answer supplies one).
Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary - describing a relationship between angles of a shape. C-7.3 rejected, recall not proof.
Two angles given, the other two in ratio 8:15 - angle-sum computation. Not C-7.3.

Asks what extra premise (DE = EF) a proof needs before SAS congruence will give CF equal and parallel to DA. The object of the question is the structure of the deductive argument, so C-7.3 and not C-4.1, even though congruence is the tool.
Assertion is a computed smallest angle (58 degrees), reason is the 360 angle sum. The work is arithmetic on angles -> C-4.1. C-7.3 rejected: no theorem is proved.

Turns on the theorem 'a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle' doing the deductive work for the assertion. C-4.1 rejected because the item is about the theorem, not about computing or classifying from given measures.

The named Class 9 theorem that a diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles. C-4.1 also mentions congruence, but here the theorem itself is the content, not congruence used to solve something.

Assertion is a property of a square (angle ABC = 90); the point of the item is that the reason about diagonals, though true, does not explain it. Property identification -> C-4.1. C-7.3 rejected, nothing is proved from axioms.
DP = PC follows only via the mid-point theorem, which the reason clause states. The theorem is what carries the argument, so C-7.3 over C-4.1.

Median produced to X with AD = DX gives a parallelogram by the converse theorem 'diagonals bisecting each other imply a parallelogram'; the reason wrongly adds 'at right angles'. Theorem-level reasoning -> C-7.3.
Consecutive versus opposite sides of a quadrilateral and how many points they share - vocabulary describing the parts of a 2-D shape. C-7.3 rejected: no theorem, no proof.
Equates two opposite angles (3x-2) and (50-x) and computes 37 degrees. Arithmetic from a stated property -> C-4.1, not C-7.3.
Angles in ratio 2:3:7:6 checked against 40/60/140/120 - angle-sum computation. Not C-7.3.
AQ = QP because the mid-point line FE meets the altitude at its mid-point - the converse mid-point theorem is doing the work, and the reason states it. C-7.3 over C-4.1 for that reason.
Angles in ratio 3:4:4:7, find all four. Computation from the angle sum, so C-4.1 rather than C-7.3.

Two consecutive angles given algebraically turn out to be 90 each, so the parallelogram is a rectangle: computation followed by classification. C-7.3 rejected - naming the special case is not proving a theorem.
One angle 30 degrees less than the smallest - solves for all four angles. Numeric, so C-4.1 not C-7.3.
'Show that it is a rectangle' from equal diagonals - a written proof using SSS congruence and co-interior angles. C-4.1 rejected: the deliverable is the argument, not a measure.
Perimeter 40 with PQ = 12 gives the remaining sides via opposite sides equal. A length computation -> C-4.1, not C-7.3.
Angle A minus angle C is 0 because opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal - applying the relationship. C-7.3 rejected.
Rhombus with angle A = 70, find B and C from opposite-equal and adjacent-supplementary. Computation -> C-4.1.
'Show that BFDE is a parallelogram' from AE = CF on the diagonal - a proof built on diagonals bisecting each other. C-4.1 rejected, no measure is sought.
'Show that F is the mid-point of BC' in a trapezium - the converse mid-point theorem written out as a proof. C-4.1 rejected.
'Show that triangle DEF is also equilateral' via the mid-point theorem on all three sides. A proof, so C-7.3.
'Show that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular' - one of the chapter's standard theorems, proved with SSS congruence and a linear pair. C-4.1 rejected.
Mid-points of a rhombus form a rectangle - a full proof combining the mid-point theorem with perpendicular diagonals. Compare sha 4e38afc2, which asks only for the condition and is therefore C-4.1.
'Prove that a diagonal bisecting one angle of a parallelogram bisects the opposite angle also' - alternate angles chained into a proof. C-4.1 rejected.
Square inscribed in an isosceles right triangle: show the opposite vertex bisects the hypotenuse, via congruent triangles CFE and BDE. A proof -> C-7.3.

'Find the length of CF' with AB = 10, AD = 6 and the bisector of angle A. The deliverable is a length, so C-4.1, even though the route uses isosceles-triangle reasoning. C-7.3 rejected on that ground.
'Prove PQRS is a rhombus' when AC = BD - mid-point theorem on four triangles. A proof, so C-7.3 not C-4.1.
'Prove that DL, DK, BM and BN enclose a rhombus' in a square, via SAS and AAS congruence. A proof -> C-7.3.
'Prove that QN = QR' by chaining isosceles-triangle and corresponding-angle equalities. A proof, so C-7.3.
'Measure the acute angle between the two diagonals' of a rectangle from a 25 degree inclination - the same numeric task as sha 2155b00d, hence the same C-4.1 call and not C-7.3.
Angle OAB from angle BOC = 90 and angle BDC = 50 - alternate angles in a parallelogram used to compute. C-7.3 rejected.
Angles in ratio 3:7:6:4 make ABCD a trapezium: computes the angles, then classifies the quadrilateral from co-interior pairs. Classification is C-4.1; C-7.3 rejected.

The quadrilateral formed by the four angle bisectors of a quadrilateral has supplementary opposite angles - identifying the figure that a construction produces, i.e. testing a conjecture. C-7.3 rejected: the MCQ asks which figure, not for the proof.
Bisectors of the angles between two parallel lines enclose a rectangle - a relationship among lines and angles, identified not proved, so C-4.1 over C-7.3.

DEQP is a parallelogram from four mid-points. Named as an MCQ outcome rather than proved, so C-4.1; contrast sha 47e03d13, where the same mid-point theorem has to justify the assertion and the call is C-7.3.

Assertion PQRS is a parallelogram, reason is the mid-point theorem, and the key is that the reason IS the correct explanation - the item tests the theorem-to-conclusion link. C-4.1 rejected for that reason.
In a rhombus the diagonal bisects the angles at both ends - a theorem, while the reason (perpendicular diagonals) is a different true theorem that does not explain it. Deductive content -> C-7.3.
'Every parallelogram is a rectangle' is false - the hierarchy of quadrilaterals. Classification of shapes -> C-4.1; C-7.3 rejected, no proof is at stake.

Properties of a parallelogram's diagonals against the equal-and-perpendicular condition for a square: property and classification -> C-4.1. (Defect: the key marks the assertion 'the diagonal of parallelogram bisects each other' FALSE, which is only defensible as a reading of the singular 'diagonal'; the stem looks garbled and the key is doubtful.)
Angles 110, 80, 70, 95 sum to 355, so the assertion fails the 360 angle sum - an arithmetic check on a stated set of angles. C-7.3 rejected.
